title: BLF: LINKTYPE_LIN has 4 or 8 bytes of payload (BUGFIX)
description:
The LINKTYPE_LIN format only allows 4 or 8 bytes as payload but not any
other length.

See https://www.tcpdump.org/linktypes/LINKTYPE_LIN.html

notes.body:
added 1 commit
  • 40288ec1 - BLF: LINKTYPE_LIN has 4 or 8 bytes of payload (BUGFIX)
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20574/diffs?diff_id=1426295707&start_sha=987eb5a804e71e6d0ec6abc0a998d510b526cde3)

> The LINKTYPE_LIN format only allows 4 or 8 bytes as payload but not any other length.

Is there any compelling reason to require that, rather than just indicating, in the spec, that it *might* be padded, but that it's not *guaranteed* to be padded. That would break precisely zero writers, and would require that readers pay attention to the `payload_length` field of the header - which they should already be doing.

In fact, it's not even clear whether the payload having two 4-octet words is meant to indicate that the payload must be an words; perhaps it's just because the author of that page chose to show the packet contents as 4-octet words, which is different from the way other pages show them.

I can redo that page.

I am not sure, why the specification requires it. As this format was first introduced by others outside of Wireshark, I am not sure. It would have been typically written by automotive data loggers - I guess that there was some optimization regarding alignment behind that. And if the format can be only 12 or 16 bytes, this might be quite simple to optimize?

When I wrote the original LIN code, I respected that padding:
https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/epan/dissectors/packet-lin.c#L480

However, in the BLF code, I seem to have missed it. :disappointed: When you now use the BLF code to write a pcap/pcapng it is not correct.

I just figured that out as I am working on the BLF writer code and stumbled over that issue as I have the LINKTYPE_LIN format in memory and need to translate back to the BLF format.

So we have two options to make it consistent:
1. change linktype specification and packet-lin.c, while risking that other implementations out will not be compatible
2. just change the blf reading

I think the later is less risky.

What do you think?

added 3 commits
  • 40288ec1...4cc01a69 - 2 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • 25f3105e - BLF: LINKTYPE_LIN has 4 or 8 bytes of payload (BUGFIX)
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20574/diffs?diff_id=1426748458&start_sha=40288ec1c4fb724af5bee5f6cee217fbb04f38e8)

> I am not sure, why the specification requires it.

Does it *require* padding, or is it just vague about it? The specification says "If a message is a LIN-Frame, the payload is a LIN N_PDU, as described in section 7.4 "Transport layer protocol data units" of ISO 17987-2:2016.", but that section doesn't appear to require that the payload's length be a multiple of 4 octets.

As this format was first introduced by others outside of Wireshark, I am not sure. It would have been typically written by automotive data loggers - I guess that there was some optimization regarding alignment behind that. And if the format can be only 12 or 16 bytes, this might be quite simple to optimize?

Optimize writing, or reading?

For the former, *allowing* padding is sufficient.

Does BLF always pad the payload to a multiple of 4 bytes?  If not, I don't see the purpose of doing so for pcap or pcapng.

> change linktype specification and packet-lin.c, while risking that other implementations out will not be compatible

Other readers, presumably - as long as we *allow* padding, we will be able to read padded packets.

I don't think that this padding comes from ISO but from Hannes Kaelber, X2E, who registered the LINKTYPE_LIN. I would assume (but I do not know for sure) that based on their products they focus on writing the files. However, we do not know how many readers were build on LINKTYPE_LIN definition. Such readers could expect the padding.

I do not see, why we would not add this padding in the BLF case.

> I do not see, why we would not add this padding in the BLF case.

Would it cause extra padding bytes to be added if, for example, you run editcap on a BLF file and write to another BLF file? If so, that doesn't seem to be useful behavior.

No.

BLF does have a different format. When we open BLF, we write the LINKTYPE_LIN format into memory for the protocol dissectors. When we write back BLF, this is converted back.
OK, I've sent Hannes an email asking whether the format specification for LINKTYPE_LIN specifies padding to 8 octets or not.
Ok. Keep in mind it does not say to pad to 8 Bytes. But to 4 or 8 Bytes.

btw: My colleague Ayoub Kaanich was getting the information from Hannes back than to write the LINKTYPE_LIN. We looked into the original Emails from that time.

We share the understanding that this is a 4 Byte alignment using padding at the end.

Situation right now:
- LINKTYPE_LIN specification
  * Calls for padding
- packet-lin.c (LINKTYPE_LIN reader)
  * Assumes that padding is present. However, proto_item_set_end will be fine, if it is not there.
  * Also if only partial padding is present. No error reported.
- blf.c reader (converts BLF to LINKTYPE_LIN in memory)
  * Does not add the padding consistently
  * If this is written to pcap/pcapng, this does not match the specification but packet_lin.c seems to cope with it.
- blf.c writer [Draft MR] (LINKTYPE_LIN to BLF in memory)
  * When it assumes padding to be present, fails when read from BLF and also pcap/pcapng without padding

We have these options:
1. Keep the specification the same
  * Keep LINKTYPE_LIN the same
  * No risk that something somewhere else breaks
  * Keep packet-lin.c the same
  * **Use this MR to clean up blf.c**
  * No need to change blf.c writer code [Draft MR]
  * Read pcap, write pcap. Keeps padding but does not add any.
  * Read blf, write blf. Always different anyhow because we loose meta data. 
2. Change LINKTYPE_LIN
  * **Change the LINKTYPE_LIN specification**
  * **Risk that there are existing implementations that break (risk not very high)?**
  * Change packet-lin.c or keep it the same?
  * Keep blf.c
  * **Change the blf.c writer code [Draft MR]**
  * Read pcap, write pcap. Keeps padding but does not add any.
  * Read blf, write blf. Always different anyhow because we loose meta data.

I do not see any benefit in going for 2. Why do you consider it?

> Situation right now:
> 
> * LINKTYPE_LIN specification
>   * Calls for padding

*Can be interpreted as calling for padding*. The problem with the specification is that it's *unclear*. The frame format, for some unknown reason, is laid out in 4-octet groups, rather than as individual fields. The words "pad" and "padding" appear nowhere in the document; all it says is that "payload[n]" is "Payload Byte n. Payload 5-8 exists only if payload_length is larger than 4."

This needs to be fixed to more clearly indicate the intent. Hannes is currently out-of-office; I will resend my message if he doesn't reply after he returns.

> * packet-lin.c (LINKTYPE_LIN reader)
>   * Assumes that padding is present. However, proto_item_set_end will be fine, if it is not there.
>   * Also if only partial padding is present. No error reported.

If no padding is present - i.e., there are exactly `payload_length` bytes in the packet, following the header - would packet-lin.c have *any* problems, and would it report anything to the user? If not, how does it assume that padding is present, rather than just *allowing* padding to be present?

> Change the LINKTYPE_LIN specification

This should be done in *any* case, to make it clearer what is required - e.g., if padding is required, at least one word with the substring "pad" should appear.

> Risk that there are existing implementations that break (risk not very high)?

If the spec is changed to explicitly *allow* padding and not *require* it, no writers will break, and only readers that behave incorrectly, or report errors, if padding is absent will break.

pcap and pcapng/ecap readers MUST NOT (in the [BCP 14](https://datatracker.ietf.org/doc/bcp14/) sense) read past the amount of data in the packet record/block, as specified by the "captured length" field of the record/block; any reader that does not do so is broken. Thus, to some degree a non-broken reader must be prepared to handle a packet with fewer than 12 octets or with 13-15 octets. (In fact, it must be prepared to handle 0 to 2^32-1 octets without crashing or reading past the end of the packet data.)

It also must use the `payload_length` to distinguish between payload and padding.

Given that, I think it unlikely that many implementations are unable to handle missing padding - if any at all are.

And given that @kayoub5 said "That being said, I never actually padded the message in my writer implementations.", there may also be files out there without padding.

> Change packet-lin.c or keep it the same?

At least from a quick look at it, the only change - *which should be made regardless of what the LINKTYPE_LIN specification says* - is to have it return `tvb_captured_length(tvb)` under *all* circumstances, so as not to falsely advertise that it's dissected data that is not present in the tvbuff.

I'll make that change and backport it to 4.4 and 4.2.

> I do not see any benefit in going for 2.

It doesn't unnecessarily pad packets.

It doesn't require readers of non-pcap/pcapng files to add padding. (As padding will probably be *allowed* in pcap/pcapng files, the *writers* of formats that don't allow padding will have to strip it off no matter which solution we choose.)

> _Can be interpreted as calling for padding_. The problem with the specification is that it's _unclear_. The frame format, for some unknown reason, is laid out in 4-octet groups, rather than as \> individual fields. The words "pad" and "padding" appear nowhere in the document; all it says is that "payload\[n\]" is "Payload Byte n. Payload 5-8 exists only if payload_length is larger than 4."
>
> This needs to be fixed to more clearly indicate the intent. Hannes is currently out-of-office; I will resend my message if he doesn't reply after he returns.

Yes.

> > * packet-lin.c (LINKTYPE_LIN reader)
> >   * Assumes that padding is present. However, proto_item_set_end will be fine, if it is not there.
> >   * Also if only partial padding is present. No error reported.
>
> If no padding is present - i.e., there are exactly `payload_length` bytes in the packet, following the header - would packet-lin.c have _any_ problems, and would it report anything to the user? If not, how does it assume that padding is present, rather than just _allowing_ padding to be present?

As I wrote it I assumed the padding is present and used `proto_item_set_end`. But this works because it checks the available bytes.

> > Change the LINKTYPE_LIN specification
>
> This should be done in _any_ case, to make it clearer what is required - e.g., if padding is required, at least one word with the substring "pad" should appear.

Yes, we need to clarify!


> > I do not see any benefit in going for 2.
> 
> It doesn't unnecessarily pad packets.
> 
> It doesn't require readers of non-pcap/pcapng files to add padding. (As padding will probably be > _allowed_ in pcap/pcapng files, the _writers_ of formats that don't allow padding will have to strip it off no matter which solution we choose.)

If the writer does not use `LINKTYPE_LIN` it will construct a new format anyhow. I do not think that stripping padding is of concern. :smile:

> As far as I know, Hannes didn't make a public implementation, and used the link type only in internal projects.

...

> Read blf, write blf. Always different anyhow because we loose meta data.

Perhaps this means that we should develop a new LINKTYPE_ for LIN, which:

1. is *not* based on internal documentation for some unknown implementation that writes out pcap files;
2. incorporates all metadata supported by BLF, and any other file formats that support LIN.

BLF can carry lots of different data not only LIN: https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/wiretap/blf.h#L741 We currently support 11 formats for LIN alone: https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/blob/master/wiretap/blf.c#L3527 And yes, we could have a "wrapper linktype" that wraps BLF, so we do not loose any information but we have different scenarios:
Scenario Today (convert to pcap linktypes) Wrapper linktype
Open BLF blf.c does the conversion on read **We need for every BLF format a dissector!** **Right now Wireshark supports \~38 formats**
Read BLF, Filter BLF, Write BLF BLF -\> pcap, filter, pcap -\> BLF Much easier
Open pcapng, write BLF The same blf.c: Conversion to BLF encapsulation needed The same blf.c: Conversion to BLF encapsulation needed
Open BLF, Write pcapng blf.c: BLF -\> pcap pcapng.c: no change **Much easier?** **blf.c: basically very simple** **pcapng.c: use wrapper linktype** **But very limited!** **However, nobody besides Wireshark understands the wrapper linktype. How to convert to pure pcapng???**
Open BLF, write something else Ok pcapng to xxx already done!? **To complicated.** **We might just block this by not supporting the Wrapper Linktype?**
I was thinking about the "wrapper linktype" approach for some time but I am afraid that the creating all format dissectors and not being able to write pcapng that someone else understands are not what we want. See the discussion of saving some meta data here: https://gitlab.com/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20525#note_2637840004

added 17 commits
  • 25f3105e...89b0311f - 16 commits from branch wireshark:master
  • 9d966d22 - BLF: LINKTYPE_LIN has 4 or 8 bytes of payload (BUGFIX)
[Compare with previous version](/wireshark/wireshark/-/merge_requests/20574/diffs?diff_id=1429554125&start_sha=25f3105ecedb12094573d87fc405f4857d3d5a08)

> BLF can carry lots of different data not only LIN:

So can pcapng. In pcapng's case, that requires different link-layer types to be on different interfaces.

> And yes, we could have a "wrapper linktype" that wraps BLF

If there are truly cases where the *same* interface can have *more than one* link-layer type, that might be appropriate.

But I'm not entirely happy with the existing LINKTYPE_ERF, and am not sure adding another such "wrapper for an existing file" link-layer type would be a good idea.

Providing link-layer types that include metadata specific to that link-layer type that is sufficient to handle most if not all needs, along the lines of [radiotap](https://www.radiotap.org) for 802.11 and the [TAP Link Type](https://gitlab.com/exegin/ieee802-15-4-tap/-/blob/master/IEEE%20802.15.4%20TAP%20Link%20Type%20Specification.pdf) for 802.15.4, would probably be the best way to go here. (And, yes, that might include an additional new type for CAN, as an added alternative to the "what you get from Linux's SocketCAN implementation" linktype we have now.)

Understood. Especially in events and errors BLF seems to cover much more than pcap/pcapng right now. I guess it makes a lot of sense to improve LINKTYPE_LIN, LINKTYPE_FLEXRAY, and maybe a new LINKTYPE_CAN to better cover those needs. But that needs a bit of research first.

I also see a need of putting "events", like a trigger event (marker by e.g. an external trigger button), link-up, link-down, etc. into a special LINKTYPE. Maybe I am missing something existing today.

One more thing: what do we do about this MR?

> Especially in events and errors BLF seems to cover much more than pcap/pcapng right now.

pcap/pcapng *plus existing link-layer types* - pcap and pcapng are the containers, the link-layer types (and block types, in the case of pcapng) define the contents.  (Most other capture file types, including BPF, can be viewed in a similar fashion, although, for most of them, the organization that defines the container format also defines the content types.)

> I also see a need of putting "events", like a trigger event (marker by e.g. an external trigger button), link-up, link-down, etc. into a special LINKTYPE.

Or, if you're willing to limit it to pcapng - which, if you have more than one LINKTYPE, you'll have to do anyway - one or more *block* types.

> One more thing: what do we do about this MR?

My inclination is to wait until Hannes Kälber gets back, ask him what was intended and whether padding needs to be mandatory or could be "allowed but not required", and proceed from there.
